Messages.Author: Todd Banister
Messages.Body:
Sorry guys, just could not let this pass....

>
> I'm sorry, I'm missing something here:

Yep.

> 1) Parnassus just isn't that nasty.
>

You ARE kidding right? Parnassus isn't that nasty? What can this vampire NOT
do?

Combat: He can take down anyone in combat with CEL and QUI (except when a
DotB or weather controls are played - grrr). I know this for a fact cause I
have been using him in almost every deck I play for the past eight months.
Just ask anyone in my group how much of a bad ass he is.

Intercept: Ummm.. Had Parnassus blocking with as much as +4 intercept before
on a few occasions. Gotta get into combat somehow. Nothing wrong here.

Bleed: Since he has access to basic tha then he can use an Infernal
Familiar. Now Parnassus can bleed for 5 per turn. I've done this many times.
Gotta block him sooner or later.

And while we are on the subject of Parnassus/Infernal Familiar: He can now
deflect, untap, have first round aggravated hand damage, prevent damage,
freak drive and even steal vampires that are in torpor. Nothing wrong here.

He can even pass votes by using Awe/Bewitching Oration and Voter
Captivation. With the backing of Alamut, Parnassus only becomes a stronger
voter.

All this from a 7 capacity Assamite.

So far I simply can not see why you would say "Parnassus just isn't that
nasty".

Maybe you have never seen anyone play Parnassus correctly. :)

Todd Banister
Prince of Atlanta
Scribe of the Assamites

Messages.Author: Todd Banister
Messages.Body:
>When looking for a bad ass with up to 7 pool to spend give me any of the following to not only be a >better vampire but one that could also kick Parnassus' ass too:

I disagree that each of the vampires that you listed can kick Parnassus' ass. Lets take a look. :)

Most of the vampires (Jimmy Dunn, Dre, Anvil, Olivia and such) that are in your list rely on massive potence strikes to deal damage. If Parnassus uses multiple diseases at the beginning of combat the opposing minion's hand damage will be reduced to say -4 to -8 for the duration of combat. Pretty tough to hurt him while he blurs back with his hand damage (and second round it becomes aggravated with Blood Agony).

Zack, Badger, and Gitane have access to protean for aggravated damage but Parnassus can once again counter with a disease(s) to take away (claws of the dead, wolf claws and such) the hand strikes and he can use acrobatics to dodge the Body of Sun or Body Flare while still striking back.

The Nosferatu vampires have a very difficult time against Parnassus due to generally not having enough manuevers to stop the long range assaults and no way to counter the multiple strikes and to deal with the aggravated damage.

The Tremere also have a difficult time against the Assamites as they can not deal with the multiple first round strikes and can not soak aggravated damage.

Several of the vampires that you listed rely on fortitude to prevent damage. Parnassus can play Blood Sweats and Theft of Vitaes at long range to get around this.

One thing that can not be stopped in combat is someone playing a DotB deck (or Weather Control) where they drop multiple DotB and the S:CE. As far as I know no one has a way to get around this. Another is when someone plays a Thoughts Betrayed to take away your strikes. Not much you can do here either.

In my original post I did not claim that Parnassus was the greatest vampire in combat. Anyone can be stopped with the right cards (but Parnassus has counters to most of the more common combat strategies). What I did say was that I did not understand why Fredrick stated that Parnassus is not all that nasty when indead he is. This is only my opinion and to each his own.



Messages.Body:
On Fri, 31 Dec 1999 22:06:46 GMT, Alex Harmon <alexh...@home.com>
wrote:

>True, it does all depend on the cards in your hand. You may be fortunate
>enough to have 3-4 disease cards in hand or enough dodges/maneuevers to
>fend off damage. Then again, I may save my cards until psyche is played
>and so on. It can go back and forth with different 'cards in hand'
>scenarios but I have found from my experience that it is usually the
>Assamite who gets the short end of the stick when it comes up against
>most of the other common combat decks.

Hm. Gun decks - get hit for agg on the first strike. Not likely to
be carrying enough maneuvers to hold close range. The Assamite can
always Dodge and Blur, but most gun decks Blur as well, so that's not
as good an idea.

Potence "big fists" combat - has no hope of outmaneuvering the
Assamites, unless you are the Brujah. Even then, probably not.

Potence frisbee combat - does 3 damage and takes some agg on the first
strike. Somewhat effective, but expensive on vampires.

Gangrel Claw decks that use DotB - Dodge, then Blur, and now it's a
question of how much prevent the Gangrel have packed, because you have
at LEAST +1 hand damage. If they aren't using DotB, they get
outmaneuvered and Blood Sweated. Body Flare is sort of expensive to
keep using, and not really seen a lot.

I really don't see this being the short end of the stick, myself. =)

>If you have success with Parnassus and can manage to help the Assamites
>win their share of games then my hat is off to you.

Winning is the trick... But in combat, the Assamites really are the
trump card. It's just managing to get them to OUST someone, instead
of just kill things.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
On Sat, 1 Jan 2000, Derek S. Ray wrote:

<snip - interesting comparison of Assamites to other combat clans>

> I really don't see this being the short end of the stick, myself. =)
>

Indeed. They seem to do *well* against other combat decks, since as you
show, they can have superior skills in many situations. They would do
'interestingly' versus Immortal Grapple, but the superior maneuverability
would mean they could go to long range and spit with aggravated damage.

My main gripe with them has tended to be their inability to do things that
the other combat clans can do much better - cope versus combat defence.
They do have a good ability to annoy Damage Prevention people, but against
dodge they fall down to the Potence crowd, who throw down Immortal
Grapple, the Gangrel, who throw Scorpion Sting, and the Tremere who
through Thoughts Betrayed. Similarly, versus Strike: Combat Ends, I find
Psyche to be a *much* weaker counterpart to the previous cards, and the
Gangrel's Dog Pack (which is rubbish, but still). There are a couple of
neat cards for the Assamites which work oddly with Psyche - I want to play
Disease to prevent you from hurting me. However, if I *do* play Disease,
you throw down Strike: Combat Ends, so I have wasted them *and* have to
play Psyche. If I don't play the Disease, you may not throw down Strike:
Combat Ends (seeing the ability to inflict a little damage on me, since
Sideslip - a highly useful but much underplayed card, IMHO - is not common
in most groups) and so I don't need to play the Psyche. Highly annoying.

> >If you have success with Parnassus and can manage to help the Assamites
> >win their share of games then my hat is off to you.
>

> Winning is the trick... But in combat, the Assamites really are the
> trump card. It's just managing to get them to OUST someone, instead
> of just kill things.

True, true. However, a few copies of Swallowed by the Night might help -
the option to maneuver and get stealth on your bleeds - with a couple of
spying Missions too. Just a few to add that extra oomph to your bleeds,
that the Brujah can't muster so easily - Alacrity is very expensive, and
weenie Brujah can't exploit Carthage Remembered.

--

James Coupe

Messages.Body:
"Derek S. Ray" wrote:

Hm.  Gun decks - get hit for agg on the first strike.  Not likely to
be carrying enough maneuvers to hold close range.  The Assamite can
always Dodge and Blur, but most gun decks Blur as well, so that's not
as good an idea.

I tend to discount gun decks altogether. In the case of them going vs an Assamite deck, well, this is a match up the Assamite would relish since gun decks are designed for maneuver/blur.

Potence "big fists" combat - has no hope of outmaneuvering the
Assamites, unless you are the Brujah.  Even then, probably not.

Brujah potence - Brujah can maneuver toe to toe with Assamites. Most Brujah decks may not be designed to use as many maneuvers however. Here it depends on deck variation. Todd Banister, when using Parnassus as an example, implied that he could play 2-4 disease, render big potence damage ineffective and thus rely less on long range to defeat Brujah. You seem to emphasize the long range angle. In either case I feel a Brujah deck could be constructed to defeat any Assamite deck since Brujah can adapt to either style (close or long range) where as Assamites basically are long rage combatants.

Potence frisbee combat - does 3 damage and takes some agg on the first
strike.  Somewhat effective, but expensive on vampires.

This plays like a gun deck and therefore doesn't match up well vs. the Assamite style. I can't imagine anyone seriously expecting to win playing this kind of deck (for a tournament let's say) though. style. I don't think it's fair to say that this deck is a common combat deck either.

Gangrel Claw decks that use DotB - Dodge, then Blur, and now it's a
question of how much prevent the Gangrel have packed, because you have
at LEAST +1 hand damage.  If they aren't using DotB, they get
outmaneuvered and Blood Sweated.  Body Flare is sort of expensive to
keep using, and not really seen a lot.

A pure claw deck is not effectively using Gangrels. There are many card combos (simple ones) that dismantle Assamites. Dotb, scorpion sting, skin of steel for example. To be even deadlier throw in any of these: carrion crows, an aggro. damage claw, dawn operation. Remember, these are just 'plain jane' combos that a Gangrel deck could pull off with regularity. Gangrels just laugh at Assamites imo.

Nosferatu are right behind Gangrel (simply for lack of fortitude). Dotb, immortal grapple, pound for X damage, repeat. Throw in carrion crows, torn signpost, fists of death, scorpion sting for spice. How difficult is that?
 
I really don't see this being the short end of the stick, myself.  =)

Again, it usually never plays out quite this simple. Maybe your maneuver intensive deck is jammed and my Jimmy Dunn gets his way with you. Maybe I don't have the dotb I packed 12 of. It could go on and on but like I said before, in most cases I just haven't seen the Assamite deck defeat other combat decks too often. I got so fed up myself that I ended up resorting to a cel/tha deck using a few of the Assamites as a way to keep their cards in play.

Just my $0.02

Certainly, you can CONSTRUCT a Brujah deck to defeat an Assamite deck
- just include enough maneuvers to catch them, and then enough POT
cards to keep your hand damage high, and then enough Blurs to actually
hurt him, and hopefully enough Tastes not to end up with your vampire
empty after tangling with him. If you include enough maneuvers to
catch the Assamites, though, you hand-jam when you're not fighting the
Assamites. It's a nasty little catch-22. I emphasize the long range
angle because, well, first round agg is great and being at long range
where you can't get poked in the eye is always nice, too. =)

>> Potence frisbee combat - does 3 damage and takes some agg on the first
>> strike. Somewhat effective, but expensive on vampires.

Hm. David Tatu had an increased strength/thrown junk deck that made
it to the finals of a tournament and gained a VP - which was then Life
Booned away from him by his grandprey. d'oh! I've got one that
doesn't do badly if the Minion Taps come out early enough. I think
it's perfectly fair to call it common - you may just not have seen it.
=)

>> Gangrel Claw decks that use DotB - Dodge, then Blur, and now it's a
>> question of how much prevent the Gangrel have packed, because you have
>> at LEAST +1 hand damage. If they aren't using DotB, they get
>> outmaneuvered and Blood Sweated. Body Flare is sort of expensive to
>> keep using, and not really seen a lot.
>>
>
>A pure claw deck is not effectively using Gangrels. There are many card
>combos (simple ones) that dismantle Assamites. Dotb, scorpion sting, skin of
>steel for example. To be even deadlier throw in any of these: carrion crows,
>an aggro. damage claw, dawn operation. Remember, these are just 'plain jane'
>combos that a Gangrel deck could pull off with regularity. Gangrels just
>laugh at Assamites imo.

Dawn Op requires a block, and the Gangrel have a little trouble with
actions you MUST block. Scorpion Sting is good, but for some reason
we don't see it much 'round here - probably because its utility
against S:CE is just not there, and it's an extra card. (Note that
one Disease stops Scorpion Sting, depending on how many Diseases
you've stuffed in your deck - 0 aggravated undodgeable hand damage is
not a worry.) Carrion Crows falls over to S:CE as well - I consider
Gangrel combat even less common than potence 'thrown stuff' combat,
just because they have NO options against S:CE. (Dog Pack is a joke.)

The real problem Assamites have is DotB combined with prevent. One
card cancelling multiple maneuvers, and the prevent that suddenly
works again at close range.

>Nosferatu are right behind Gangrel (simply for lack of fortitude). Dotb,
>immortal grapple, pound for X damage, repeat. Throw in carrion crows, torn
>signpost, fists of death, scorpion sting for spice. How difficult is that?

Without getting your Nossie killed? Very. one Disease removes enough
of the hand damage so you don't get him in the first smack. The Blur
that will follow with the +1 hand damage will do 6 points total. The
Taste of Vitae that will follow gains back all the blood he lost, and
NOW Carrion Crows does its damage - after it doesn't matter anymore.

However, if you want something amusing, use the Nosferatu Law Firm -
DotB, Grapple, Torn Signpost, Pushing the Limit, Skin of Steel. Blood

s.net>, Derek S. Ray <lor...@yahoo.com> writes

>Without getting your Nossie killed? Very. one Disease removes enough
>of the hand damage so you don't get him in the first smack. The Blur
>that will follow with the +1 hand damage will do 6 points total. The
>Taste of Vitae that will follow gains back all the blood he lost, and
>NOW Carrion Crows does its damage - after it doesn't matter anymore.

Carrion Crows, as far as I can tell, follows the same template as Wolf
Companion et al. As such, the damage done occurs during the *first*
strike resolution step, not the last - since you cannot guarantee that
after the first strike resolution step there will be another, even if
you say "Oh, but I'm going to Blur."
